{"id": "27:36/q05", "question": "What does 'are you supplying me with wealth?' mean?", "turns_on": "The surface question states financial support; the bribery reading uses the preceding demand for submission and the following threat to explain its purpose.", "positions": [{"id": "27:36/q05/p1", "position": "Solomon reproaches their attempt to add wealth to his resources, since he needs none of it.", "reasons": "Al-Farrāʾ's imdād is additional supply; Abū Zayd distinguishes supplying people from other senses of extension; Bursevī says the verb takes its second object with bi. Al-Rāzī, Abū Ḥayyān and al-Samīn stress the interrogative's rejection and disdain."}, {"id": "27:36/q05/p2", "position": "The gift is an attempted bribe to make Solomon tolerate the queen's rule and unbelief.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr says Solomon wanted Islam or force, not treasures; Ibn ʿĀshūr ties the bribe to the queen's unanswered demand for submission in 27:31. {"id": "27:36/q07", "question": "What was the queen's gift?", "turns_on": "The reports list different contents; al-Zajjāj's inference from māl favors monetary value.", "positions": [{"id": "27:36/q07/p1", "position": "It included money, gold, or silver.", "reasons": "Al-Zajjāj infers money from Solomon's word māl; Ibn ʿĀshūr says gold and wealth seem likely. Al-Māwardī adds the Himyarite royal staff and the request for water from neither sky nor earth. Al-Ālūsī recalls these reports."}, {"id": "27:36/q07/p3", "position": "It included male and female attendants, horses, and other worldly goods.", "reasons": "Wahb ibn Munabbih, Yazīd ibn Rūmān and Ibn Lahiʿa specify attendants, Arabian or fine-bred horses; Ibn Lahiʿa gives one hundred horses. {"id": "27:36/q08", "question": "Why is the offered wealth called 'māl' without specification?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "27:36/q08/p1", "position": "Its indefinite form belittles the offer against Solomon's God-given resources.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī and al-Ṭabāṭabāʾī explicitly draw this from the indefinite; Bursevī adds that māl is passing acquisition, also called ʿaraḍ, citing al-Mufradāt's saying that wealth moves from house to house."}]}
{"id": "27:36/q09", "question": "What Arabic sound rules bear on the alif of māl?", "turns_on": "Sībawayh's examples weigh kasra, yāʾ, emphatic articulation, distance, case ending and pause; these are general phonetic analogies, not a reported variant of this verse.", "positions": [{"id": "27:36/q09/p1", "position": "The alif can incline toward imāla where an underlying yāʾ or kasra favors it.", "reasons": "Sībawayh lists māl with nāb and bāʿ as alifs standing where yāʾ could stand; some imale māl in genitive or all cases by analogy with Mālik. Stable forms like ʿimād and ʿābid differ from case-varying māl. Rāʾ with kasra after an alif can favor imāla even against an earlier emphatic; imāla of kāfir is more common than qādir, which Hudbah's verse attests. He notes variation in kāfir, manābir, fār, ḥimār, dinānīr, ʿimrān, ʿafran, and related forms."}, {"id": "27:36/q09/p2", "position": "Emphatic consonants, proximity, word form, and pause can block or weaken imāla.", "reasons": "Sībawayh says seven emphatics raise the tongue and block imāla adjacent to or after alif, even across intervening letters; ṣaqt for sabaqt illustrates articulatory accommodation. Earlier kasra can counter a more distant emphatic, with qifāf versus miṣbāḥ and rare ʿirqan/ḍīqan analogies. Particles usually resist imāla unless named; ba, ta and vocative yā are special. Geminate fāʿil, mafāʿil and hollow forms resist it. Rāʾ acts like a doubled sound and blocks or permits inclination according to case, distance and neighboring qāf; at pause the lost kasra no longer inclines dāʿ. Fatḥ is favored in fāriq and firāsh."}]}
{"id": "27:36/q10", "question": "What is the force of the initial fa in 'what God gave me'?", "turns_on": "Whether fa versus a hypothetical wāw encodes the addressees' ignorance or only links the explanation; al-Samīn challenges the inference.", "positions": [{"id": "27:36/q10/p1", "position": "Fa makes God's superior gift the consequent explanation for Solomon's rebuke.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says it gives the reason and consequence; al-Nasafī and al-Zamakhsharī contrast a hypothetical wāw, which would presuppose the envoys already knew Solomon's wealth, whereas fa informs them. Ibn ʿĀshūr adds that the queen apparently did not know."}, {"id": "27:36/q10/p2", "position": "The proposed contrast between fa and wāw is insufficiently demonstrated.", "reasons": "Al-Samīn questions whether the particle alone conveys the addressees' knowledge and asks why Solomon attributes the gifts to God rather than merely saying he is richer."}]}
{"id": "27:36/q11", "question": "What is the grammatical role of mā in the comparison?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "27:36/q11/p1", "position": "Mā is a relative pronoun: what God gave Solomon is better than their wealth.", "reasons": "Bursevī parses it as a relative pronoun, making the whole clause the subject of the comparison."}]}
{"id": "27:36/q12", "question": "What is 'what God gave me'?", "turns_on": "Whether God's comparative gift denotes spiritual office plus kingdom, material wealth alone, or inward knowledge. Al-Ālūsī weighs the first as more fitting.", "positions": [{"id": "27:36/q12/p1", "position": "It is God's gifts of prophethood, religion, wisdom, kingship, and material power.", "reasons": "Muqātil includes Islam, prophethood and troops; al-Thaʿlabī adds wealth and wisdom; al-Nasafī includes blessing. Ibn Kathīr adds vast wealth and forces, and Asad includes insight into hidden realities. Al-Ālūsī prefers prophethood and unique sovereignty as primary; al-Nasafī argues religion brings lasting benefit and he already has ample goods."}, {"id": "27:36/q12/p2", "position": "It can be understood chiefly as Solomon's material wealth.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī allows the reading but finds it less eloquent and contextually weaker than prophethood plus sovereignty."}, {"id": "27:36/q12/p3", "position": "In an inward reading, it is certain knowledge, sacred realities, intellectual delight, and luminous vision.", "reasons": "Al-Qāshānī contrasts these with sensory and imaginary adornments."}]}

{"id": "27:36/q16", "question": "What does the turn with بَلْ do?", "turns_on": "Whether bal is described as a move to their motive, to the practical refusal, or to exclusive contrast.", "positions": [{"id": "27:36/q16/p1", "position": "It moves from rejecting the money to explaining the offer by their worldly motive.", "reasons": "Al-Bayḍāwī, al-Nasafī, al-Samīn and al-Ālūsī say Solomon exposes the only sort of gain they recognize; Ibn ʿĀshūr says it also indirectly refuses and returns the gift."}, {"id": "27:36/q16/p2", "position": "It signals a contrast: only they rejoice in the gift, while Solomon does not.", "reasons": "Al-Suyūṭī says the definite subject and affirmative predicate restrict rejoicing to them after his rejection. Ibn ʿĀshūr likewise says fronting antum makes the gift impress them alone."}]}

{"id": "27:36/q18", "question": "Why do they rejoice in the gift?", "turns_on": "Whether 'your gift' attaches to recipient or giver, whether joy is literal pride or ironic return, and whether the sentence states motive or spiritual contrast.", "positions": [{"id": "27:36/q18/p1", "position": "They love receiving gifts and accumulating worldly goods; Solomon does not.", "reasons": "Muqātil says people rejoice in exchanged gifts, whereas Solomon wants Islam. Ibn ʿĀshūr says the predicate indirectly announces the return."}, {"id": "27:36/q18/p5", "position": "They expect a larger material or political return from sending a ruler a gift.", "reasons": "Al-Ālūsī reports that the hoped-for return could include sparing their country from destruction."}]}
{"id": "27:36/q19", "question": "Why is أَنتُم placed before 'rejoice'?", "turns_on": "Whether word order or explicit subject alone yields restriction; some notes make context decisive.", "positions": [{"id": "27:36/q19/p1", "position": "Fronting the subject restricts rejoicing to them and excludes Solomon.", "reasons": "Al-Suyūṭī says a definite subject with affirmative predicate can restrict; al-Sakkākī supports explicit subjects and fronting, while Ibn ʿĀshūr applies the restriction directly. {"id": "27:36/q20", "question": "What did Solomon display and solve before returning the gift?", "turns_on": "The narrative reports differ in objects, numbers, methods, and the envoys' identity.", "positions": [{"id": "27:36/q20/p1", "position": "He solved the box, bead, staff, water, and disguised-attendant tests, then sent the gift back.", "reasons": "Muqātil says Gabriel disclosed the box and horse sweat supplied the water. {"id": "27:36/q24", "question": "What general syntactic patterns do the accompanying grammar excerpts illustrate?", "turns_on": "These notes give general grammar examples without applying them to the syntax of 27:36.", "positions": [{"id": "27:36/q24/p1", "position": "After aw, a subjunctive may rely on unspoken an; a raised verb may coordinate or begin a new clause.", "reasons": "Sībawayh gives aw in the sense 'unless' with Imruʾ al-Qays, Ziyād and al-Ḥuṣayn. Dhū al-Rumma and Ṭarafa illustrate raised alternatives. Al-Khalīl parses al-Aʿshā's alternatives; Yūnus favors a fresh clause and Sībawayh calls it easier for 42:51. Zuhayr illustrates strained semantic coordination, and ʿAmr ibn Maʿdīkarib supplies a comparison idiom."}, {"id": "27:36/q24/p2", "position": "A verb between conditional jussives may substitute for or describe the first act; conjunctions normally keep it jussive.", "reasons": "Sībawayh uses Zuhayr, al-Ḥuṭayʾa, al-Aṣmaʿī's report, and al-Khalīl on 25:68-69 to distinguish explanation, circumstantial description, and independent raising. He rejects semantically unrelated substitutions except as speech slips. Thumma/fa/waw/aw govern a linked jussive; al-Khalīl allows weak accusative after fa/waw via implicit an but prefers jussive. Completed conditions allow independent raising; 3:111, 47:38, 2:284, 2:271 and 7:186 illustrate case distinctions. Tense and negation affect acceptable responses."}, {"id": "27:36/q24/p3", "position": "Commands, questions, wishes, offers, and prohibitions can govern jussive results when a conditional relation is intended.", "reasons": "Sībawayh and al-Khalīl explain the implicit in-condition and causal test. 61:10-12, 15:3, 6:91, 20:77, 14:31, and 39:64, plus poetry of Jābir, al-Akhṭal and Ṭarafa, illustrate jussive, circumstantial and independent raised alternatives. Actual past facts are not conditional; a noncausal following clause may be raised; rare noun-like complements and an-infinitives are noted."}]}
{"id": "27:36/q25", "question": "What general textual, rhetorical, and transmission observations occur in the accompanying excerpts?", "turns_on": "These are source excerpts with no expressed application to a particular word of 27:36.", "positions": [{"id": "27:36/q25/p1", "position": "Abū Jaʿfar's recitation has early Medinan transmission and standing.", "reasons": "Ibn Mujāhid traces it through Ibn ʿAyyāsh to Ubayy and the Prophet; Ibn Abī al-Zinād and Yaʿqūb ibn Jaʿfar praise his proficiency and Ibn ʿAbbās connection. Abū Jaʿfar recalls teaching before 63 AH, following Ibn ʿAyyāsh's muṣḥaf, and Umm Salama's blessing. Ibn Mujāhid says he records additional ʿĀṣim variants at their locations."}, {"id": "27:36/q25/p2", "position": "Sound pairing and rhyme are effective when wording remains apt to meaning.", "reasons": "Al-Jurjānī lists tajnīs pairs and good sajʿ in prayer, prose and sayings; Prophetic sayings supply examples. A Bedouin's rhymed complaint used precise rukāb, as al-Jāḥiẓ argues against substituting other camel terms."}, {"id": "27:36/q25/p3", "position": "The verb sharā can name either side of a property exchange.", "reasons": "Ibn al-Jawzī says a buyer gives the price and seller the good; sharā is an antonymic term and in the cited other verse means selling."}, {"id": "27:36/q25/p4", "position": "Some Quranic words can have foreign origins yet be Arabic by naturalized usage.", "reasons": "Abū ʿUbayd reconciles both descriptions; al-Jawālīqī and Ibn al-Jawzī favor his account."}, {"id": "27:36/q25/p5", "position": "The Quran's eloquence uses apt words and innovative prose styles beyond poetry and soothsayer rhyme.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr discusses context-sensitive literal and figurative choice, semantic and syntactic subtlety, and varied expression. {"id": "28:8/q01", "question": "What does the opening fāʾ leave unstated?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:8/q01/p1", "position": "It follows an omitted account of Moses' mother nursing him and casting him into the river.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān supplies nursing and casting; Bursawī recalls the command and her protection of the chest; Ālūsī says the deletion conveys her prompt obedience."}]}

{"id": "28:8/q08", "question": "Who was Pharaoh?", "turns_on": "Reports differ over Pharaoh's name and origin.", "positions": [{"id": "28:8/q08/p1", "position": "He was al-Walīd ibn Muṣʿab.", "reasons": "Ibn Isḥāq, reported by Ibn Abī Ḥātim, calls him unusually rebellious, outspoken, and long-reigning."}, {"id": "28:8/q08/p2", "position": "He was a non-Arab from Hamadhān.", "reasons": "Ibn Abī Ḥātim reports this from al-Ḥasan."}, {"id": "28:8/q08/p3", "position": "He was Persian, from Istakhr.", "reasons": "Nasafī reports this from al-Zajjāj."}]}
{"id": "28:8/q09", "question": "What is the lām in ليكون doing?", "turns_on": "Whether the expressed end belongs to the family's intention, a figurative presentation of the unintended outcome, or God's intended decree; some propose omitted or reordered syntax.", "positions": [{"id": "28:8/q09/p1", "position": "It marks the unintended consequence of taking Moses in: he later became their enemy and grief.", "reasons": "Ibn Qutayba says they took him as a son; Ṭabarī, Ibn Isḥāq, Zajjāj, Ṭabrisī, and others contrast their hope of benefit or comfort with the ruin that followed. Zajjāj compares wealth leading to death; Māwardī and poets compare birth and nurturing for death and building for ruin. Rāzī invokes 28:9, 20:39, and 7:179. Zarkashī says consequence still truthfully expresses causation and cites a proposed substitution of fa. Abū Ḥayyān supplies the omitted nursing sequence. Iṣlāḥī says they were unaware Moses would end Pharaoh's rule."}, {"id": "28:8/q09/p2", "position": "The purposive lām is figurative or ironic: the result is represented as if it motivated the family's act.", "reasons": "Zamakhsharī compares conventional purpose expressions and Rāzī prefers his account, using a lion metaphor. Bayḍāwī, Biqāʿī and Ibn ʿĀshūr likewise identify an imagined motive; Ibn ʿĀshūr calls it a dependent metaphor and differs from Sakkākī. Sāmin allows this or a consequence lām; Itqān calls it a derivative metaphor in the particle. Ālūsī reports a literal purpose with implicit comparison and rejects the objection that pickup is involuntary because taking and care were deliberate. Ālūsī reports Sakkākī and Taftāzānī's relation-level metaphor; Khaṭīb al-Dimashqī instead starts from a comparison involving the genitive, which ʿAbd al-Ḥakīm prefers because lām's meaning depends on it."}, {"id": "28:8/q09/p3", "position": "The lām expresses God's intended decree and wisdom in their taking Moses.", "reasons": "Ibn Kathīr prefers this from 28:6: God made their precautions fail. ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz cites God's prior promise and knowledge. Zarkashī argues an outcome lām suits an ignorant agent but God's acts carry wisdom; speaking of the family's act heightens regret. Ālūsī rejects supplying an explicit 'He decreed the taking so that...' as unsuitable."}, {"id": "28:8/q09/p4", "position": "A literal purpose can be supplied: they took him for fear he would become an enemy.", "reasons": "Itqān reports Abū Ḥayyān's preferred omitted noun, and Ibn al-Dahhān proposes their aversion to that outcome as the motive."}, {"id": "28:8/q09/p5", "position": "On an unusual reordered parsing, 'enemy and grief' is a circumstance and they took him to possess him.", "reasons": "Zarkashī reports Ibn al-Dahhān's rearrangement without adopting it."}]}
{"id": "28:8/q10", "question": "How does the purpose construction work grammatically?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "28:8/q10/p1", "position": "Lām governs a subjunctive verb through an understood verbal noun or kay.", "reasons": "Naḥḥās calls ليكون accusative under the purpose lām and dismisses weak grammarians' objections. Zarkashī says kay may be understood with lām and discusses its occurrence with or without lām. Ibn ʿĀshūr identifies lām kay governing a verbal noun understood from an plus the subjunctive, ordinarily denoting the agent's motive."}]}
{"id": "28:8/q11", "question": "In what sense would Moses become their enemy and grief?", "turns_on": "Whether enmity concerns religion and destruction generally or distinct effects on men and women.", "positions": [{"id": "28:8/q11/p1", "position": "He would oppose their religion and bring grief through their defeat and destruction.", "reasons": "Qatāda speaks of religious opposition and what befell them; Muqātil specifies destruction and anger over firstborn, connecting 26:55. {"id": "28:8/q12", "question": "To whom does لهم refer across Moses' later life?", "turns_on": "Whether the pronoun denotes the initial household narrowly or a continuing dynasty.", "positions": [{"id": "28:8/q12/p1", "position": "It refers to Pharaoh's ruling house, state, or nation, including a later Pharaoh.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr says the Pharaoh whom Moses opposed was later than the one whose household found him."}, {"id": "28:8/q12/p2", "position": "It refers to the household that found and raised him.", "reasons": "Most accounts speak of the rescuing household becoming the target of his enmity and their own loss; no separate generational distinction is made."}]}
{"id": "28:8/q13", "question": "Why call Moses himself grief?", "turns_on": "Whether the verbal noun directly intensifies the description or has an omitted 'for them' relation.", "positions": [{"id": "28:8/q13/p1", "position": "It emphatically calls the cause of grief 'grief' itself.", "reasons": "Bursawī and Ālūsī say the wording intensifies sorrow; Ṭabāṭabāʾī calls grief the cause by figurative intensification."}, {"id": "28:8/q13/p2", "position": "It is a verbal noun with an omitted relation, meaning grief for them.", "reasons": "Ibn ʿĀshūr rejects analysis as a source noun used adjectivally for emphasis and calls the attribution to Moses a causal metaphor."}]}

{"id": "28:8/q19", "question": "What does خاطئين say about Pharaoh, Haman, and their troops?", "turns_on": "Whether khāṭiʾīn names deliberate sin and its punishment or their disastrous misjudgment; several sources allow both.", "positions": [{"id": "28:8/q19/p1", "position": "They were culpable sinners, especially for unbelief, shirk, and oppression; God made them raise their destroyer as punishment.", "reasons": "Yaḥyā calls them polytheists; Wāḥidī, Ṭabrisī, Qurṭubī, and others say disobedient. {"id": "28:8/q20", "question": "What is the distinction between khaṭiʾa and akhṭaʾa?", "turns_on": "Whether the forms distinguish intent and culpability or overlap in Arab usage.", "positions": [{"id": "28:8/q20/p1", "position": "Khaṭiʾa is deliberate culpable sin; akhṭaʾa or mukhṭiʾ refers to unintended error.", "reasons": "Abū Ḥayyān contrasts intentional khāṭiʾ and mukhṭiʾ; Bursawī describes a person intending good but slipping. {"id": "28:8/q23", "question": "What does the verse teach about God's decree and Pharaoh's precautions?", "turns_on": "The notes emphasize distinct facets of divine decree: the fixed outcome, Moses' protection, and punishment for oppression.", "positions": [{"id": "28:8/q23/p1", "position": "God's prior knowledge and decree made Moses Pharaoh's enemy despite Pharaoh's precautions.", "reasons": "ʿUmar ibn ʿAbd al-ʿAzīz argues against a Qadari claim that Pharaoh could have supported Moses, invoking 20:43 and the promise in 28:6. {"id": "28:15/q07", "question": "What does 'fighting' describe and what were the men doing?", "turns_on": "Whether the post-indefinite verb is an adjective or an allowable circumstantial clause.", "positions": [{"id": "28:15/q07/p1", "position": "The verb clause qualifies the two men; they were fighting one another.", "reasons": "Al-Samin and Al-Alusi prefer adjectival attachment; Bursevi explains reciprocal form; Ibn Ashur says the fighting was severe mutual beating and Biqai describes grappling, strangling, and striking."}, {"id": "28:15/q07/p2", "position": "The clause is circumstantial: Moses found them while they fought.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya gives this parse; al-Samin notes that Sibawayh permits circumstantial clauses from indefinite nouns more broadly than most grammarians."}]}
